Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arjun Mehta was 37 when he came for treatment, a married South Asian American man who worked as a psychologist and spoke with some embarrassment about how strange it felt to be sitting on the other side of the room. The event he returned to when he tried to explain what had happened was a terrorist attack that had taken place months earlier during an evening professional meeting held in a downtown office building. It had run late, and by the time people began leaving it was fully dark outside. He remembered the ordinary details with painful clarity: the stale conference coffee, the scrape of chairs, the sense of being tired and ready to go home to his wife. Then the first gunshots cracked through the lobby below. For a second he had not understood what he was hearing. Then came shouting, another burst of shots, and the sound of people running.

What stayed with him most was not only the noise but the absolute loss of control. He and others dropped to the floor and tried to barricade themselves in a side room. He could hear shots in uneven bursts and footsteps in the hallway, and he remembered the humiliating certainty that nothing he knew, professionally or personally, could help him. He had no way to protect anyone, no way to predict where the attacker was, no way to make the situation stop. In the darkened room, lit only by the thin light under the door, he had waited for what felt like hours, listening for movement and trying to keep his breathing quiet. He said that was the moment the world changed shape for him: it no longer felt basically structured or negotiable, but abruptly dangerous.

In the weeks that followed, those impressions stayed close to the surface. If he woke in the night and the bedroom was dark, he would feel a jolt of alarm before he was fully conscious, as if he were back in that room listening for someone outside the door. A gunshot sound in a movie, a car backfiring on the street, even a sharp cracking noise at a distance could stop him cold. He was not describing these as abstract reminders; in the moment, his body acted as if the threat were present again. He became acutely uncomfortable in situations where he could not set the terms or control what was happening. Delays, crowded public places, other people changing plans suddenly, being stuck in traffic after sunset—each left him keyed up and scanning for exits.

Arjun had come to believe that bad things could happen without warning and that he could not stop them. He said this plainly, but it also appeared in the way he moved through his life. He began avoiding anything that felt potentially stressful, not because he thought of himself as fragile, but because he could not bear the sense of being overwhelmed or trapped. At work, he narrowed his schedule and turned down speaking engagements that would have kept him in the office after dark. He found reasons not to attend evening department events. As a psychologist, he was used to sitting with other people's fear, but now, if a patient began describing violence in vivid detail late in the day, he noticed himself wanting to end the session quickly and get home before nightfall. He was ashamed of that. The person he had become felt unrecognisable to him—cautious, avoidant, easily thrown, someone who mentally checked escape routes in buildings he had entered hundreds of times before.

At home, his wife saw him drift away even when he was physically present. He described slipping into elaborate private fantasy, letting his mind float into a world of his own when conversations became difficult or when the evening quiet made him tense. Sometimes she would ask him a question and realize he had not heard a word she said. He had also started drinking more than he used to, and at times used medication or other substances to blunt himself enough to sleep or to get through the night without feeling so alert to every sound. He did not present this as reckless so much as necessary; in his mind he was trying to create distance from a world that no longer felt safe.

Over time these habits constricted his life. His wife had begun going to social events alone because he almost always found a reason not to go. At work he remained competent, but colleagues noticed he was less available, less willing to stay late, more likely to cancel if a day already felt too full. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent night when he woke in a dark room during a brief power outage and, before he could orient himself, felt the same helpless terror he had felt during the attack. The next morning he told his wife he could not keep living as if danger were everywhere and as if he were no longer himself. What frightened him most was the idea that this was now permanent—that the world would always seem dangerous, and that he would remain a man organized around avoiding the next bad thing he was certain he would not be able to stop.
